  • e Context of the Fragment ad ĪPK 1.5.4-5:
  • e Debate between a Vijñānavādin and a Sautrāntika
  • d the Problem of the Other Conscious Streams
  • ĪPK 1.5.4-5,12 Utpaladeva lets a Sautrāntika criticize the
  • jñānavādins’ idealistic thesis that the universe is merely an internal
  • rm taken on by consciousness and that phenomenal variety is the result
  • an internal mechanism of latent traces or imprints (vāsanā). In the
  • urse of this criticism, not only does the Sautrāntika attack the
  • jñānavādins’ position regarding the status of the external object:13
  • also argues that the Vijñānavāda can only lead to solipsism, since in
  • e Vijñānavādin’s perspective, other subjects must be mere internal
  • pects of my own stream or series (santāna) of momentary cognitive
  • ents. I have examined elsewhere the details of this controversy,14 so
  • re I shall only give a basic summary of it.
  • e Vijñānavādin denies the accusation of solipsism by using
  • armakīrti’s line of argument in the Santānāntarasiddhi.15 According to
  • armakīrti, just as in a system that admits the reality of entities
  • ternal to consciousness, in the idealistic system of the Vijñānavāda,
  • e other streams of consciousness cannot be directly perceived (since a
  • nsciousness cannot be directly apprehended by another consciousness
  • t only by itself); yet, just as in a system that accepts the reality
  • external entities, in the Vijñānavāda, the other streams of
  • nsciousness can be inferred. This inference of the existence of other
  • nscious entities or streams of momentary cognitions rests on the fact
  • at we experience in ourselves that when we act (and for instance when
  • speak), our action is preceded by a will to act. So when we witness
  • action that has not been preceded by our own will to act, we can
  • fer that this action was preceded by a desire to act that does not
  • long to our own stream of cognitions – and this other willing entity
  • st be another conscious subject.
  • this argument the Sautrāntika replies that the Vijñānavādin’s own
  • esuppositions prevent him from making the very inference that he
  • fends. He thus shows that the Vijñānavādin has no means of
  • tablishing the invariable concomitance on which his inference of other
  • nscious streams rests. For indeed, I can observe an invariable
  • ncomitance between my own speech and my previous desire to speak, so
  • at the logical pervasion (vyāpti) between “I want to speak” and “I am
  • eaking” is established; but in the case where I hear a speech that is
  • t uttered by me, my thought does not take the form “I am speaking” but
  • e form “he/she is speaking”. Now, the Vijñānavādin has no way of
  • tablishing any invariable concomitance between the thought “I want to
  • eak” (in someone else’s conscious stream) and the thought “X is
  • eaking” (in my conscious stream when I hear someone else speaking).
  • e two propositions “I want to speak” and “I am speaking” are
  • sentially linked to the subject, or they are not “separated”
  • icchinna) from the “I”, whereas the proposition “X is speaking” is
  • parated from the “I” since it is expressed by using the third
  • ammatical person, and we have no way of determining that there is a
  • usal relationship (kāryakāraṇabhāva) between somebody else
  • bjectively thinking “I want to speak” and our own objective16 thought
  • is speaking”, so that the cause of the phenomenon “X is speaking”
  • mains perfectly unknown.
  • e Vijñānavādin replies that in fact this necessary relation between
  • e subjective cognition “I want to speak” and the objective cognition
  • is speaking” is constantly apprehended in the ordinary world, because
  • r actions are always related to our awareness that they can be
  • tnessed by others: when we act, we act while desiring either to be
  • en acting or not to be seen acting, but whether we conceal our actions
  • whether we act ostentatiously, we are aware that our desire to act
  • es not merely result in the cognition “I am acting” (which occurs in
  • conscious stream) but also in the cognition “X is acting” (which
  • curs in the other conscious streams witnessing my action). And
  • cording to the Vijñānavādin, it is thanks to this understanding of the
  • variable concomitance between my subjective desire to act and the fact
  • at my action becomes an object of cognition for the others that the
  • ference of other conscious streams is possible.
  • e following passage of the Vivr̥ti begins with the Vijñānavādin’s
  • planation of this very argument, after which Utpaladeva (or, as
  • hinavagupta says, the Īśvarādvayavādin, the “proponent of the thesis
  • the non-duality [of the universe] with the Lord”) helps the
  • utrāntika criticize the Vijñānavādin’s position. Utpaladeva points out
  • at this position entails a logical circle, because our awareness of
  • e existence of other conscious entities is supposed to stem from our
  • areness that the others can witness our actions, while our awareness
  • at the others can witness our actions must derive from our awareness
  • the existence of other conscious entities. He also points out that in
  • ct there is no such thing as an invariable concomitance between the
  • bjective thought “I want to be heard by others” and the objective
  • ought “X is speaking”, because we sometimes experience that we can
  • eak without being heard whether we want it or not: thus the causality
  • lationship invoked by the Vijñānavādin between a subjective will to
  • t and the objective awareness that X is acting cannot be established.
  • e Śaiva non-dualist concludes from this that the other subject can
  • ly be established when the other’s action is perceived both by him/her
  • n the form “I want to speak/I am speaking”) and by me (in the form
  • e/she is speaking”), from the supposition that the same action is then
  • prehended in these two different forms. For we have to make this
  • sumption in order to justify the unity of the sphere of human practice
  • yavahāra): if we do not accept it, then we cannot justify our belief
  • at the other subjects share with us the same spatio-temporal
  • terminations and therefore live in a common world, and the notion of
  • tersubjectivity collapses.
  • Abhinavagupta makes clear in his commentary, the Śaiva non-dualists
  • ve a solution to this problem of intersubjectivity:17 according to
  • em, the unity of the sphere of human practice is to be explained as
  • e result of the constant activity of division and synthesis through
  • ich the universal consciousness appears to itself in the form of
  • veral distinct subjects and yet is capable of unifying these subjects
  • terms of spatial and temporal determinations, because although it
  • nifests itself as plural, it remains fundamentally one, just as a
  • eaming consciousness is capable of dividing itself into a multiplicity
  • characters without losing its unity. Recognizing the others is
  • erefore understood by Utpaladeva as a partial “recognition of the
  • rd” (īśvarapratyabhijñā), i.e. as the incomplete realization of the
  • namism inherent in consciousness: when I witness an activity that is
  • t mine in the world, I recognize in that activity a freedom that is
  • thing but the essence of my own subjectivity, so that my awareness of
  • e existence of other subjects is not the result of an inference based
  • causality (“another conscious entity must have produced this
  • tion”): rather, it arises from an inference based on the identity of
  • ture (svabhāva) between the freedom to act and consciousness.
  • netheless, in the Vivr̥ti fragment below, this solution remains mostly
  • plicit,18 because the Śaiva non-dualist is almost immediately
  • terrupted (at least if we follow Abhinavagupta’s commentary)19 by the
  • utrāntika, who takes advantage (or at least thinks he does so) of
  • paladeva’s criticism of the Vijñānavāda so as to put forward his own
  • sition. He agrees with the Śaiva non-dualist that the Vijñānavādin
  • ils to explain the spatio-temporal determination (avadhāra) of the
  • her subjects (a reproach that Vasubandhu had already faced in his
  • ṁśikā)20 and he points out that the only option left to the
  • jñānavādin trying to infer the existence of other subjects is to admit
  • at the thought formulated as “I want to act/I am acting” in one given
  • nscious stream projects an image of itself in another conscious stream
  • n image that takes the form “he/she is acting”): the other subject
  • st be inferred as the reflected object (bimba) producing in my
  • nscious stream the reflection (pratibimba) “he/she is acting”, just as
  • particular reflection in a mirror presupposes the existence of a
  • flected object which exists outside of the mirror and gives it its
  • rticular shape.
  • first sight, this theory must be appealing to the Vijñānavādin
  • ponent as it seems to fit his idealism: if he adopts it, he can admit
  • e existence of several conscious streams projecting reflections of
  • emselves onto each other without conceding the existence of external
  • jects. As a matter of fact, there is evidence in several Yogācāra
  • xts that at least some Buddhist idealists held this thesis and used it
  • as to explain the fact that several subjects seem to perceive the
  • me objects: according to those texts, the objects apprehended by the
  • nses must be reflecting an “original” object in the ālayavijñāna,21
  • d this “original” object is in turn a reflection of images occurring
  • other conscious streams.22 This idea that the phenomenal variety
  • perienced in one conscious stream is the result of the influence of
  • other conscious stream rather than of an external object is found in
  • rticular in Vasubandhu’s Viṁśikā23 (demonstrably known of Utpaladeva
  • d Abhinavagupta).24
  • course, such an explanation is not without danger for the
  • jñānavādin, since as the Sautrāntika points out in Abhinavagupta’s
  • V, acknowledging the existence of entities distinct from my own
  • gnitive stream (be they other conscious streams) seems to pave the way
  • r externalism.25 But whereas in the ĪPV, the Sautrāntika apparently
  • rgets in a general way any idealistic thesis that concedes the
  • istence of a plurality of conscious streams while denying the reality
  • anything external to them, in the fragment presented here, he seems
  • have in mind, more specifically, the idealistic contention that
  • enomenal variety can be explained as a result of the mutual influence
  • various conscious streams; and he shows that such a thesis leads to
  • absurd consequence, since each conscious stream should then perceive
  • infinite number of objects, just as (according to Abhinavagupta’s
  • age) several mirrors reflecting each other produce an infinite number
  • reflections.
  • e fragment ends on an objection made by the Vijñānavādin. The latter
  • adily accepts that all the other manifestations contained in other
  • nscious streams do not project reflections of themselves onto my
  • nscious stream (he agrees that this would lead to an absurd
  • nsequence), but he argues that some of these manifestations in other
  • nscious streams awaken a particular imprint (vāsanā) already contained
  • my own conscious stream and left by previous experiences. He thus
  • es the theory of the vāsanā mechanism to explain why we only perceive
  • limited number of objects.
  • fortunately, the end of the discussion (won by the Sautrāntika, at
  • ast in this part of the treatise) is missing. This is all the more
  • grettable since in the corresponding passage of the ĪPVV,
  • hinavagupta alludes to a very interesting discussion on ālayavijñāna26
  • an important topic for the historian of Buddhist doctrines, and one
  • at is not found in Utpaladeva’s ĪPK and Vr̥tti, nor in Abhinavagupta’s
  • V, but that may well have been treated in some detail in Utpaladeva’s
  • vr̥ti.
  • netheless, the fragment as it stands is of great interest, not only
  • cause it confirms once again how faithful Abhinavagupta’s ĪPVV is to
  • e text on which it comments (all the ideas mentioned in the
  • rresponding passage of the ĪPVV are to be found in the Vivr̥ti), or
  • cause it confirms interpretations of the ĪPV that were so far only
  • sed on the ĪPVV,27 but also because it illustrates Utpaladeva’s
  • timate acquaintance with Buddhist theories in general,28 and his
  • terest for the Buddhist debate over the epistemological (and/or
  • tological)29 status of other streams of consciousness in particular.
  • e reason for this interest probably lies in the fact that Utpaladeva’s
  • stem is a variety of absolute idealism: according to him, the universe
  • nothing but a manifestation of a single and all-powerful
  • nsciousness out of which nothing exists. He therefore shares with the
  • jñānavāda the burden of dealing with the accusation of solipsism, and
  • is all the more attentive to this problem since he wants to offer a
  • lution capable of superseding both that of the Vijñānavādins and that

  • fore showing (as he will in the following verses) that the Sautrāntika
  • ew regarding both objects and other subjects is untenable.30 His
  • urce regarding the Vijñānavādins’ position in this fragment is in all
  • obability Dharmakīrti’s Santānāntarasiddhi (a treatise that was read
  • the Śaiva philosophers, whether dualist or non-dualist).31 As for his
  • urce regarding the Sautrāntika opponent, it is difficult to judge to
